candidate_analysis.explanation: The Random Forest assigns a malware probability of 1.0000, and all 20 top features have positive SHAP values (+0.0067 to +0.0152) toward cryptojacking. However, the evidence is diffuse and mostly generic. No single feature dominates: the top contribution is only +0.0152, and the 20 contributions form a smooth, shallow gradient. The highest-frequency n-grams (MOV PUSH at 0.0376, ADD PUSH at 0.0325, PUSH CALL at 0.0291, CALL PUSH at 0.0142, LEA PUSH at 0.0069, SUB PUSH at 0.0044) are stack-based argument-passing and call-setup sequences. These are typical of ordinary 32-bit x86 compiled code and are not specific to mining. Several rare n-grams are more distinctive: PUSHFD POP, POP XCHG, POP XOR, POP SUB, POP TEST and CALL RET. They are unusual, low-frequency pairings that could indicate hand-written, obfuscated, packed or shellcode-like code, but they could also come from library or compiler idioms. DIV MUL, MOV FLD and CDQ MOV point to arithmetic and numeric-conversion code (integer division/multiplication, x87 floating point, sign extension). That is compatible with compute-heavy routines but not diagnostic of hashing or mining. LEA MOVSD.REP suggests block memory copying. No function names or locations were provided for any n-gram, and no mining-specific constructs appear in the evidence. The model's output strongly favors malware, but the n-grams alone cannot show cryptojacking behavior specifically. The result is suspicious but inconclusive, so I classify it as low-confidence.

Call followed by a push at 0.0142. It reflects a dense call-heavy, stack-based calling convention and is generic.
Frequent (0.0325) pointer or value arithmetic before a push. It is part of the generic stack-argument profile shared with many programs.
Extremely rare (0.000027) pop followed by subtraction. It is somewhat unusual and could come from hand-written or obfuscated code, but this is not conclusive.
Rare (0.000054) call immediately followed by return, i.e. a tail-wrapper or thunk-like stub. It is mildly unusual structure with no direct mining link.
Very rare (0.000014). Pop followed by exchange is atypical for compilers and may reflect hand-crafted, packed or obfuscated code, but the evidence is weak at this frequency.
Common (0.0291) argument push before a call. It confirms a stack-based calling convention and is generic.

Saving the flags register and then popping it is uncommon in ordinary compiled code. It can appear in low-level or obfuscated routines and is one of the more suspicious rare patterns, though it is not mining-specific.
Extremely rare (0.000014) pop followed by XOR. XOR is common in hashing and obfuscation, but at this frequency and without context it is only weakly suggestive.
Pushing a computed address (0.0069), typical when passing buffer or string pointers. It is generic.
Rare (0.000095) register shuffling between stack operations. It is possibly from hand-written or stub code, with low specificity.
Very rare pop followed by a test of the popped value. It suggests a check on a returned or restored value and is non-specific.
Loading a value into the x87 FPU stack (0.0025). It indicates floating-point computation, which could come from numeric or benchmarking-style code but is not a mining signature.
Address computation followed by a repeated string move, i.e. a block memory copy or initialization. It is common in many programs and non-specific.
Rare (0.000122) pop followed directly by a call. It may indicate indirect-call setup or a stub, with limited diagnostic value.
Rare (0.000054) division and multiplication in sequence. It suggests modular or arithmetic computation, which fits compute-intensive code, but the evidence does not tie it to hashing or mining.
Register restore followed by a move (0.0013). It is generic epilogue or stack-handling code.
